extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural philosophy / scientific method; historians/philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Bacon's catalog of 'prerogative instances' and related methodological criteria for discovering forms (causal natures) in natural philosophy. Useful for designing inductive investigations and selecting decisive experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of heat (theoretical/relational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat is an expansive motion restrained, and striving to exert itself in the smaller particles; the expansion is modified by its tendency to rise, and the effort is active and somewhat violent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: Compare fire with time (time acts slowly attacking minute particles so no perceived heat); gold dissolves without great heat because penetration is mild, iron dissolves with vehement heat because penetration is violent; some gangrenes and mortifications produce little heat due to gentle putrefaction. Use these contrasts to isolate the form (the operative essence) of heat as restrained expansive motion. Caveat: consider relative (universal) form, not merely sensory impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative definition of heat (experimental test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one excites a dilating or expansive motion in any body and restrains that motion so it is partially exerted and partially repressed, heat will be produced regardless of the material's other qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: attempt to produce a dilating motion and partially repress it (i.e., prevent full expansion) in diverse substances (earthy, animal, vegetable, mineral, air, oil, water). Sensible heat corresponds to this definition relative to the senses. Use this as an operational criterion when designing experiments to demonstrate heat in non-obvious media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative instances (overview of remaining helps)
rubrics_metrics.description: A programmatic list of methodological aids for induction: 1) prerogative instances; 2) supports of induction; 3) correction of induction; 4) varying investigation by subject; 5) prerogative natures for investigation; 6) limits of investigation; 7) application to practical purposes; 8) preparations for investigation; 9) ascending and descending axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this outline to structure a full induction: begin with select instance types, use supports and corrections, adapt the investigation to subject-matter, and proceed toward axioms and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitary instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit the required nature in subjects that have nothing in common with other subjects except that nature, or that do not exhibit it where others do—thus isolating the nature clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use solitary instances to accelerate exclusion and confirmation because a few such instances can be as valuable as many common ones. Examples: prisms, dews, crystalline gems as solitary instances for color; veins of white and black in marble. They help deduce that color depends on light incidence and texture rather than intrinsic material. Scoring note: high weight for sharpening hypotheses about a nature because they remove confounding similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migrating instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the required nature passes toward generation (appears) or toward corruption (disappears); often one instance provides both phases (on passage and at opposite conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They both hasten exclusion and narrow the putative form by showing what is gained or lost in migration. Example: powdered glass and froth (generation of whiteness) vs. dissolving froth or snow (loss of whiteness). Caution: avoid attributing the form to its efficient cause (e.g., assuming air is always necessary for whiteness). Remedy by rigorous exclusion to prevent false attribution to vehicles or concomitants. Also include migrations of increase/decrease (e.g., wetting paper reduces whiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous instances (coruscations, predominant instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its fullest, most striking form—emancipated from impediments and manifest at greatest power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They make the form evident but can mislead; always follow with exclusions. Examples: the thermometer for expansion (strikingly shows air expansion), quicksilver as a conspicuous instance of weight (shows weight predominates in quantity of matter rather than density). Use conspicuous instances to perceive the bare substantial shape of a nature but beware of being deceived by what forces the form forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clandestine instances (twilight instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its lowest, initial, or weak state—concealed and subdued by contrary natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for discovering genera and broader unifying natures because they point to common underlying tendencies rather than dominant manifest forms. Examples: water bubbles, eaves' drippings, froth and snow as weak consistency in fluids; magnet armed with iron revealing latent cohesion in iron. Emphasize observation in small portions/miniature where clandestine traits are more evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive (collective) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that constitute a species or lesser form of the required nature: particular forms that collect groups of instances into a common notion and aid in definitions and partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to construct useful divisions/species en route to the greater form but avoid prematurely taking these partial forms as final (avoid stopping the inquiry). Examples for memory: (1) separation of infinity (order), (2) connection of mind with senses (commonplaces), (3) impression in passion, (4) impression when mind is pure, (5) multitude of handles (writing, recitation), (6) anticipation. For taste: constitutive instances show taste as partly internal smelling and an exquisite touch. Use constitutive instances to form intermediate hypotheses and taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar or proportionate instances (physical parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances showing resemblances and connections of things in the concrete—physical analogies that trace relations among parts of the universe and point toward broader constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are less directly helpful for discovering simple forms but valuable for revealing the architecture of nature and suggesting higher axioms (e.g., similarity between mirror and eye). Use them to build analogical reasoning about organs, motions, and large-scale relations. Caution: restrict to deep, substantial resemblances, not superficial or mystical sympathies (reject natural magic-style analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular instances (irregular, heteroclite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances exhibiting a subject as extraordinary or extravagant relative to its species—'miracles' of species that agree little with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They provoke inquiry, correct habit-induced errors, and often lead to discovering underlying forms or causes when their seeming exceptionality is analyzed. Examples: the sun and moon among heavenly bodies, the magnet among minerals, quicksilver among metals. Use them to maintain investigative curiosity and to challenge complacent generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviating instances (errors of nature, monsters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances showing nature deviating from its ordinary course (monstrous or erroneous individuals), differing from singular instances because they are deviations of individuals, not species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable for practice/operative arts because elucidating the cause of deviation can allow art to reproduce or vary known species. Collect careful, credible histories of monsters and prodigies with rigorous selection; avoid superstition and unreliable reports (cf. Livy, natural magic). Use these to learn the latent processes that lead to variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bordering instances (participants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that are intermediate or composed of two species—rudiments between one species and another; rare but instructive for understanding orders and constitutions of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They indicate possible transitions and mixtures that reveal how species relate and can point to what is possible between established species. Examples: moss (between putrescence and plant), certain comets (between stars and ignited meteors), flying fish and bats (between fishes/birds and birds/quadrupeds). Treat them as distinct class for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of power (the fasces, masterpieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works or artifices that are most noble and perfect in art—masterpieces of human workmanship that illustrate controlled application of nature and thus suggest paths to new discoveries or improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine perfected works of art/technology because they make clear modes of effecting results and often offer immediate routes to advancement or transfer to novel ends. Use them to elevate understanding and as practical stepping-stones from observed natural forms to human-directed application.
